680.title: Diwali: the row of lamps
680.hook: Rama comes home after fourteen years, and a whole city lights lamps to show him the way
680.howItsDone: In much of South India, Deepavali is celebrated before dawn on Naraka Chaturdashi with an oil bath, new clothes, firecrackers and sweets; in many other regions that day is a smaller lamp-lighting the day before the main Diwali night.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-EIGHTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Navaratri, one Goddess in nine forms. Nine nights, then the dawn.
screen: `NINE NIGHTS, THEN THE DAWN.`

segments.voice: In Tamil Nadu, a family's Deepavali can begin around four in the morning. Someone wakes the house while it's still pitch dark. Each person sits down, and an elder rubs warm sesame oil into their hair. Then a hot bath, new clothes, a firecracker before sunrise, sweets for breakfast. In North India, Diwali is usually a night: the lamps come out after dark, for Rama coming home. Same festival name. Different hour, different story. This one isn't about Rama at all.
screen: `FOUR IN THE MORNING.` → `WARM OIL, A HOT BATH, NEW CLOTHES.` → `A DIFFERENT STORY.`

segments.voice: The story belongs to Krishna and a demon king named Naraka, and the Bhagavata Purana tells it. Naraka has grown arrogant and cruel. He has stolen treasures from the gods, among them the earrings of Aditi, mother of the gods, and he holds thousands of young women captive in his fortress city. Krishna flies there on Garuda, his wife Satyabhama beside him, breaks through the fortress walls, and kills Naraka in battle. Then come two moments worth noticing. The Earth herself, Naraka's mother in the story, returns the stolen treasures and asks Krishna to protect Naraka's son. And Krishna frees the women held in the fortress, sixteen thousand one hundred in the Bhagavata's count. In the text they choose him as their husband, and he sends them to Dvaraka and marries them all. Many families add that Naraka, dying, asked for the day of his death to be remembered with lights. That's the day before the main Diwali night, Naraka Chaturdashi, the fourteenth day of Naraka. In much of South India, it is Deepavali, kept before dawn, and the oil bath, people say, recalls Krishna bathing after the battle. So the row of lamps has more than one road leading to it. In Ayodhya's story, the lamps guide a king home. In this one, a fortress breaks open and thousands of women walk out, free, toward home. Both light the way out of the dark.
screen: `NARAKA: A CRUEL KING, A FORTRESS.` · `KRISHNA AND SATYABHAMA ON GARUDA.` · `THE CAPTIVES WALK FREE.` · `NARAKA CHATURDASHI: BEFORE DAWN.` · then, large: `MORE THAN ONE ROAD HOME.`

segments.voice: Light one small light, or simply picture one. Think of someone who is stuck somewhere, in a hard job, an illness, a lonely stretch, and picture your light at the door of that place, showing a way out. Hold them and the light together, without needing to fix anything.
Diwali. In much of the South, Deepavali comes before dawn on Naraka Chaturdashi, remembering Krishna's victory and the captives set free.
screen: `DIWALI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: light the way home. Sometimes a door opens from the outside. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 680 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: HOLI: THE FESTIVAL OF COLORS.`

681.title: Holi: the festival of colors
681.hook: Prahlad walks out of the fire unharmed; the next morning everyone throws color and nobody is a stranger
681.tomorrow: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
681.howItsDone: In the Braj region around Mathura and Vrindavan, Holi is celebrated over a week or more, with Lathmar Holi in Barsana and Nandgaon, flower Holi in Vrindavan's temples, and songs of Krishna and Radha; elsewhere many families tell both Prahlad's story and Krishna's.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Deepavali before dawn in the South, and Krishna breaking open Naraka's fortress. Light the way home.
screen: `LIGHT THE WAY HOME.`

segments.voice: A little boy runs to his mother, upset. Why is Radha so fair, he asks, and I'm so dark? It isn't fair. His mother, smiling, has an idea. Go and color her face, she says, any color you like. Then you'll match. The boy is Krishna, the mother Yashoda, and that small story, told and sung all over the Braj country where Krishna grew up, is one of the reasons people there say Holi began.
screen: `WHY IS SHE FAIR AND I'M DARK?` → `GO AND COLOR HER FACE.` → `KRISHNA'S COLOR.`

segments.voice: Braj is the region around Mathura and Vrindavan, south of Delhi, where Krishna's childhood stories are set. In Braj, Holi isn't one day; it's a season of a week or more. In Barsana, the village tradition remembers as Radha's, there's Lathmar Holi, Holi of the sticks. Men from Nandgaon, Krishna's village, come over to throw color, and the women of Barsana meet them with long sticks, playfully beating them while the men hide under shields and everyone sings. The next day, it happens the other way around in Nandgaon. In Vrindavan's temples, there's a day when priests throw flower petals over the crowd instead of powder. And everywhere, songs of Krishna and Radha and the cowherd girls, the gopis, drenching each other with colored water; poets in Braj Bhasha, the local language, wrote many of them over the centuries. The Prahlad story and the Krishna story don't compete. Many families tell both: the fire the night before, for Prahlad, and the colors the next day, which in Braj belong to Krishna. Underneath the play, the Krishna story is about a boy who notices a difference between himself and someone he loves, and it bothers him. The answer isn't to argue. It's to throw color until nobody can tell who's fair and who's dark, who's from Barsana and who's from Nandgaon. Under all the color, the faces are level.
screen: `BRAJ: KRISHNA'S COUNTRY.` · `LATHMAR HOLI: STICKS AND SHIELDS.` · `PETALS IN VRINDAVAN'S TEMPLES.` · `PRAHLAD'S FIRE, KRISHNA'S COLOR.` · then, large: `UNDER THE COLOR, THE FACES ARE LEVEL.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you feel slightly apart from: a different age, different politics, a different background. Picture both your faces covered in the same bright pink powder, so nobody could say which is which. If there's a small grudge between you, let it slide off with the color.
Holi. In Braj it's Krishna's season of color, with sticks in Barsana and petals in Vrindavan, and every face the same bright mess.
screen: `HOLI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: everyone's the same color today. Under the powder, nobody's a stranger. That's day six hundred eighty-one.

screen: `DAY 681 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: MAHA SHIVARATRI: THE GREAT NIGHT OF SHIVA.`

682.title: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
682.hook: a night kept awake, water poured over the lingam, Om Namah Shivaya until dawn
682.tomorrow: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection
682.howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri many Hindus keep vigil at Shiva temples through the night, chanting and offering water, milk and bilva leaves to the lingam; some connect the night with Shiva drinking the poison from the churned ocean.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Holi in Braj, Krishna's colors, sticks in Barsana and petals in Vrindavan. Everyone's the same color today.
screen: `EVERYONE'S THE SAME COLOR TODAY.`

segments.voice: Look closely at many images of Shiva, and his throat is a darker blue than the rest of him. It isn't a painting mistake; it's a scar, of a kind. One of his names is Nilakantha, the blue-throated. And one story people tell about Maha Shivaratri is how his throat got that color: a moment when the whole universe nearly ended, and one god drank the danger so everyone else could live.
screen: `A BLUE THROAT.` → `NILAKANTHA.` → `THE NIGHT HE DRANK THE DANGER.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata Purana tells it in its eighth book. The gods and the demons, usually enemies, agree to work together for once. They want amrita, the nectar of immortality, at the bottom of the ocean of milk. So they churn the ocean, the samudra manthan, with the mountain Mandara as the churning stick and the great serpent Vasuki as the rope, gods pulling one end, demons the other. But the first thing that rises isn't nectar. It's poison: Halahala, so strong its fumes spread in every direction and begin to burn the worlds. Gods, demons, every creature, run to Shiva. The text says Shiva looks on them with compassion, and his wife, the Goddess, agrees. He gathers the poison in his palm and drinks it. And in the telling many know, he holds it in his throat. He doesn't swallow it all the way down, where it would destroy him and the world inside him, and he doesn't spit it out, where it would destroy everyone else. He keeps it right there, and his throat turns blue. Some devotees connect Shivaratri to that night: the gods stayed awake, singing to Shiva, so the poison wouldn't overcome him. It's one explanation among several, but it fits the vigil. The night isn't only about staying up. It's about keeping someone company while they hold something hard.
screen: `THE CHURNING OF THE OCEAN.` · `FIRST, NOT NECTAR, BUT POISON.` · `SHIVA DRINKS IT.` · `HELD IN THE THROAT: NILAKANTHA.` · then, large: `KEEP COMPANY WITH THE ONE WHO HOLDS IT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you're holding that you can't swallow and can't spit out: a worry, a hard conversation coming, a grief. Don't push it down or away; let it sit in the throat or the chest while you breathe around it. Keep it company, the way the gods kept Shiva company.
Shivaratri. The great night of Shiva, the blue-throated one, who held the world's poison so others could live.
screen: `SHIVARATRI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: stay awake for what matters. Tomorrow, a thread tied during a losing war. Day six hundred eighty-two, done.

683.title: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection
683.hook: a sister ties a thread on her brother's wrist, and he promises to look after her
683.carry: a thread can hold a promise
683.tomorrow: Janmashtami: the night Krishna was born
683.howItsDone: On Shravana Purnima, besides sisters tying rakhis on brothers, many priests tie protective threads on the wrists of the families they serve while reciting a short Sanskrit verse remembering King Bali; in some communities the same day is also when men renew their sacred thread.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shivaratri, and Shiva's blue throat, the poison held so others could live. Stay awake for what matters.
screen: `STAY AWAKE FOR WHAT MATTERS.`

segments.voice: Before rakhis came with glitter and cartoon characters, a protective thread was serious business. Priests in many parts of India still go house to house on the full moon of Shravana, tying a plain thread on the wrists of the families they serve, with a short Sanskrit verse. The verse mentions a demon king. And behind the custom, the Puranas tell of a war the gods were losing, and a wife who tied the thread.
screen: `A PRIEST AT THE DOOR.` → `A PLAIN THREAD, A SHORT VERSE.` → `A WAR THE GODS WERE LOSING.`

segments.voice: The story is told in the Bhavishya Purana. Indra, king of the gods, has been fighting the demons a long time, and he's losing, worn out and afraid. His wife, Shachi, also called Indrani, goes to the gods' teacher, Brihaspati, for help. He tells her: on the full moon of Shravana, prepare a raksha, a protective thread, with the proper rites, and tie it on Indra's wrist. She does. Indra goes back into battle with the thread on his arm, and this time he wins. Notice who ties it: a wife, not a sister. The thread protects whoever it's tied on, and it can be tied by a wife, a priest, a sister, a friend. Now, the priests' verse. It remembers the demon king Bali, who was bound by Vishnu. Its sense: with the thread that bound the mighty Bali, king of the demons, I bind you; stay firm, O protection, stay firm. Bali is remembered as generous and honorable, and in some tellings his binding is also a kind of being held safe, with Vishnu guarding his door. So the verse asks the thread to hold the person the way Bali was held. For many families today, the thread on a brother's wrist carries all of it at once: a priest's blessing, a wife's courage, a sister's love, and a promise that doesn't need many words.
screen: `INDRA IS LOSING THE WAR.` · `SHACHI TIES THE THREAD.` · `A WIFE, A PRIEST, A SISTER, A FRIEND.` · `THE VERSE: AS BALI WAS BOUND.` · then, large: `A THREAD CAN HOLD A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who protected you without making a fuss about it: a parent who waited up, a friend who stood beside you, a stranger once. Picture a thread running from your wrist to theirs, and breathe along it. Then think of one person you'd protect, and let the thread run to them too.
Rakhi. A thread of protection, tied in the old story by Shachi on Indra's wrist, and today by sisters, priests and friends.
screen: `RAKHI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a thread can hold a promise. Tomorrow, a baby nobody could hold. See you then.

684.title: Janmashtami: the night Krishna was born
684.hook: a prison at midnight, a river that parts, and a baby carried across it to safety
684.howItsDone: Many Hindus keep the day after Janmashtami as Nandotsava, Nanda's festival, remembering the cowherds' joy in Gokul with music, sweets and gifts; in many places Yogamaya is honored as the Goddess who protected the infant Krishna.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: rakhi, and the thread Shachi tied on Indra's wrist. A thread can hold a promise.
screen: `A THREAD CAN HOLD A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: Krishna's birth is usually told as the story of one baby: the boy carried across the flooded river. But Vasudeva didn't come back from Gokul empty-handed. He laid his son beside the sleeping Yashoda and picked up her newborn daughter, then walked back through the storm to the prison, and the doors locked behind him. In the morning, Kamsa would come for the eighth child. And the eighth child, now, was a girl.
screen: `THE BABY CARRIED BACK.` → `YASHODA'S DAUGHTER.` → `KAMSA COMES IN THE MORNING.`

segments.voice: The baby cries, and the guards run to tell the king. Kamsa rushes in. Devaki begs him: you've killed my sons; this is a daughter, she can't hurt you, let me keep just this one. He doesn't listen. In the Bhagavata's telling, he grabs the baby by the feet to dash her against a stone, and she slips out of his hands. She rises into the air, no longer a newborn: the Goddess, eight-armed, holding weapons, shining. The text calls her Yogamaya, Vishnu's own power, who had agreed to be born to Yashoda for exactly this night. From the sky she tells Kamsa: killing me does you no good. The one who will end you has already been born, somewhere else. Then she's gone. And the Bhagavata does something surprising. Kamsa, shaken, apologizes to Devaki and Vasudeva for killing their children and frees them from their chains. It doesn't last; by the next day his advisers have talked him back into cruelty. But for one moment, the tyrant is sorry. Meanwhile in Gokul, Yashoda wakes to find a baby boy beside her. The cowherds throw a huge celebration, with music, gifts, and butter and yogurt splashed everywhere, and many families still keep the day after Janmashtami as Nandotsava, Nanda's festival, in memory of it. So the midnight good arrives twice: once as a boy carried to safety, once as a girl who couldn't be held.
screen: `DEVAKI BEGS FOR HER DAUGHTER.` · `SHE SLIPS FROM KAMSA'S HANDS.` · `YOGAMAYA: THE GODDESS IN THE SKY.` · `KAMSA, FOR ONE MOMENT, IS SORRY.` · then, large: `THE GOOD ARRIVES TWICE.`

segments.voice: Dim the light or close your eyes, and sit in the dark a moment. Wait for the good you don't expect: not the one you've been hoping for, but the quiet one, the side door, the thing nobody mentions. If nothing comes, that's fine; the waiting is the practice.

685.title: Ganesh Chaturthi: welcoming Ganesha home
685.hook: clay Ganeshas are carried home with drums, kept for days, then given back to the water
685.carry: welcome it, then let it go
685.tomorrow: Navaratri: nine nights of the Goddess
685.howItsDone: On the last day of Ganesh Chaturthi, often Anant Chaturdashi, families perform a final aarti, offer food for the journey, ask forgiveness for any lapse as hosts, and carry the image to water, chanting Ganpati Bappa Morya, pudhchya varshi lavkar ya.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Janmashtami, and the baby girl who rose from Kamsa's hands. The good arrives at midnight.
screen: `THE GOOD ARRIVES TWICE.`

segments.voice: The tenth day. The streets that welcomed Ganesha with drums are full again, louder than before. Trucks carry giant pandal images inch by inch toward the sea. Families carry small ones in their arms; kids ride on shoulders. And over everything, one call, shouted by huge crowds at once, in Marathi: Ganpati Bappa Morya! The crowd answers with the second half, the part that surprises people. It isn't goodbye. It's come back soon.
screen: `THE TENTH DAY.` → `GANPATI BAPPA MORYA!` → `NOT GOODBYE. COME BACK SOON.`

segments.voice: The full call goes: Ganpati Bappa Morya, pudhchya varshi lavkar ya. Ganpati, our dear father, Morya: next year, come early. Bappa is an affectionate Marathi word, like dad. Morya is often linked to Morya Gosavi, a devoted Ganesha saint remembered at Chinchwad near Pune, whose name became part of the cry. So in one breath, the crowd calls Ganesha family, remembers a devotee, and asks him to hurry back. The last day of the big festival is Anant Chaturdashi, the fourteenth. Before the image leaves home, the family gathers for a final aarti, offers him food for the road, often curd rice or modaks, and asks forgiveness for anything they did wrong as hosts. At the water's edge, the image is turned to face the house or the crowd one last time, then carried in and slowly let go. People cry at this, grown men too. Ten days ago he was clay from a shop; now losing him feels like seeing off a relative at the station. That's the heart of it: love for something doesn't depend on keeping it. The whole ritual is built around loving the guest fully, letting him go fully, then looking forward. The word visarjan is often translated immersion, but its root sense is closer to letting go, releasing. And the crowd's answer to letting go isn't despair. It's: come back soon.
screen: `BAPPA: DEAR FATHER.` · `MORYA: A SAINT'S NAME IN THE CRY.` · `FOOD FOR THE ROAD, AND FORGIVENESS.` · `LOVE DOESN'T DEPEND ON KEEPING.` · then, large: `COME BACK SOON.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who left recently: a visit that ended, a friend who moved, a child back at school. Picture the moment at the door and, before they go, thank them silently for coming. Then, on an out-breath, say inwardly what the crowd says: come back soon.
Ganesh Chaturthi. It ends with visarjan, a final aarti, food for the road, and the cry Ganpati Bappa Morya: come back soon.
screen: `GANESH CHATURTHI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: welcome it, then let it go. Goodbye can sound a lot like come back soon. Until tomorrow.

686.title: Navaratri: nine nights of the Goddess
686.hook: Durga meets the buffalo demon; nine nights of dancing, and on the tenth day the good wins
686.howItsDone: Navaratri ends on Vijayadashami: many North Indian towns stage the Ramlila and burn Ravana's effigy on Dussehra; in Bengal, Durga's image is immersed after sindoor khela; in the South, families honor tools on Ayudha Puja and many children begin learning to write.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ganesh Chaturthi's farewell, Ganpati Bappa Morya. Welcome it, then let it go.
screen: `COME BACK SOON.`

segments.voice: On the same autumn day, in three corners of India, three different things are happening. In a Delhi park, a crowd watches a giant paper-and-bamboo Ravana, taller than a house, as someone fires a flaming arrow into it. In Kolkata, married women smear red sindoor on each other's faces, laughing and crying, before an image of Durga about to leave for the river. In a Kerala home, a small child writes their first letters in a plate of rice. It's all one day: the tenth.
screen: `A BURNING RAVANA IN DELHI.` → `RED SINDOOR IN KOLKATA.` → `FIRST LETTERS IN KERALA.`

segments.voice: The tenth day after the nine nights is Vijayadashami, the victory tenth. In much of North India it's called Dussehra, and it belongs to Rama. For the nine nights before, many towns stage the Ramlila, the whole Ramayana acted over many evenings. On the tenth day, Rama defeats Ravana, and huge effigies of Ravana, often with his brothers Kumbhakarna and Meghanada, are burned. In Bengal, the same day is Bijoya Dashami, the end of Durga Puja. The Goddess, who people there say has been visiting her parents' home with her children, goes back to Shiva. Before her image is carried to the river, women offer her sweets and sindoor, then smear it on one another, a custom called sindoor khela. Afterward people embrace and visit, and the young touch the feet of the old. In much of the South, the ninth and tenth days honor tools and learning. On Ayudha Puja, people clean and decorate their tools, books, vehicles, even laptops, and set them before the Goddess. On Vijayadashami, especially in Kerala, many small children begin their education, writing their first letters in rice or sand with an elder guiding their finger. One day, three victories: the good over Ravana, the Goddess over Mahisha, the mind over not-knowing. And this week has been full of nights ending in dawn: Diwali before sunrise in the South, Holi's colors in Braj, the blue throat, Shachi's thread, a baby girl who couldn't be held, a farewell that means come back, and now the tenth day.
screen: `VIJAYADASHAMI: THE VICTORY TENTH.` · `DUSSEHRA: RAVANA BURNS.` · `BIJOYA: DURGA GOES HOME.` · `FIRST LETTERS WRITTEN IN RICE.` · then, large: `NINE NIGHTS, THEN THE DAWN.`

segments.voice: Place in front of you, or picture, one tool you use every day: a pen, a phone, your own hands. Look at it the way people on Ayudha Puja look at their tools, with thanks. Then name one small thing you won't let win tonight, and let the breath carry a quiet decision.
Navaratri. Nine nights that end on Vijayadashami: Ravana burned in the North, Durga's farewell in Bengal, tools and first letters honored in the South.
screen: `NAVARATRI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: nine nights, then the dawn. A child's first letter counts as a victory too. Day six hundred eighty-six, done.
